items.title: Why a broken JSON body is a 500
items.body:
The route calls `await request.json()` inside its `try`, before `parseSchema` ever sees anything. A body that is not valid JSON makes `request.json()` throw a `SyntaxError`. In the `catch`, `apiError` maps only `AppError` instances to their own status; anything else becomes **500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR**. The auth doc ran this case (finding F1) and sketches a `readJson` helper that would return 400.

- *400* is the right answer for the fix, not for this code.
- *422* is wrong: `parseSchema` is never reached.
- *401* is wrong: authentication already passed in `withAuth`.

items.title: Why a non-collaborator sees 404
items.body:
For a MEMBER, every note query is scoped by `buildAccessibleNoteWhere`, which requires a collaborator row for the caller. A member without one gets no result from `findAccessibleById`, and `getNoteDetail` throws **404 NOTE_NOT_FOUND**. The route gate table explains why: a member cannot tell "exists but not shared with me" from "does not exist".

- *403* would confirm that the note exists.
- *200 read-only* is wrong: there is no access at all without a collaborator row.
- *401* is wrong: the user is signed in; `withAuth` passes.

excerpts.quote: if (!note) { throw appError("This note was not found for your account.", 404, "NOTE_NOT_FOUND");

items.title: Why an editor cannot share
items.body:
Sharing requires `canManageSharing`, which `getNoteAccessLevel` sets to `isOwner`: true only for an OWNER row or the `Note.ownerId` user. An EDITOR row has neither, so `assertCanManageSharing` throws **403 FORBIDDEN** "Only the owner or an application admin can change collaborators." This happens before the target email is looked up.

- *Editors may add viewers* is wrong: there is no partial sharing right.
- *404 USER_NOT_FOUND first* is wrong: the email lookup comes after the capability check.
- *422 for a non-VIEWER grant* is wrong: the schema accepts every permission; the refusal is about the caller.

excerpts.quote: "Only the owner or an application admin can change collaborators.",

items.title: A read outside the transaction cannot see the write inside it
items.body:
Inside the save callback, the conditional update and the audit row go through `db`, the transaction client. The re-read that becomes the response goes through `findAccessibleById`, which has no `db` parameter and always uses the shared client. That query runs on a different pooled connection, and under PostgreSQL's READ COMMITTED it sees only committed rows, so it returns version 3. The workspace prints the response's version number, so the user reads Saved version 3. even though version 4 is in the database. A refetch a moment later brings version 4 into the cache, which hides the bug everywhere except the message.

- *Version 4 from the transaction client* is what passing `db` would give.
- *Version 4 after a refetch* gets the order wrong: the message is set from the response first.
- *The conflict message* belongs to the 409 branch; this was a 200.

readMore.why: The repo's own finding about this method and the transaction.

items.title: Two copies of the history, one unbounded and one unused
items.body:
Each detail response embeds the eight newest revisions, because the shared detail include says `take: 8`. The history panel ignores them. It renders the separate revisions query, whose repository method has no limit, so a note with 500 revisions sends all 500 to the browser every time that query runs, and every detail response, including the response to each save and share, still carries eight revisions nobody reads.

The usual design is one paged endpoint for history (cursor on versionNumber, a page size such as 20) and a detail payload that leaves history out.

- *The newest 8 from the detail* is what the include holds, not what the panel renders.
- *All 500 from the detail* contradicts `take: 8`.
- *The revisions route's take* does not exist.

items.title: Why archiving an archived note is a 409
items.body:
`updateStatus` first checks `canArchive`, which the owner has. It then compares the current status with the requested one; when they are equal it throws **409 INVALID_STATUS_TRANSITION** with "This note is already archived." Nothing is written. The same guard has a gap the findings call out: two concurrent archive requests that both read ACTIVE both pass it and both write (F5).

- *200 with a second audit row* is what the race can produce, not a sequential repeat.
- *403* is wrong: owners keep `canArchive` on archived notes.
- *422* is wrong: ARCHIVED is a valid `NoteStatus`.

excerpts.quote: if (note.status === nextStatus) { throw appError( `This note is already ${nextStatus.toLowerCase()}.`, 409, "INVALID_STATUS_TRANSITION",

items.title: A draft keyed to a version the cache does not have
items.body:
The editor shows the draft only while the draft's version number equals the cached note's. The conflict branch replaces the draft with `latestNote` and gives it version 6, but nothing updates the cached detail, which still says version 5: the save hook has no `onError`, and the branch invalidates nothing. The two numbers no longer match, so the editor falls back to the cached version 5 text. The user's typing is gone, version 6 is not on screen despite the message, and Save is disabled because the editor is not dirty. Typing again starts a new draft from version 5, so the next save is refused again.

The fix is one line in the branch: write `latestNote` into the cache, or invalidate the detail, before resetting the draft.

- Nothing loads version 6, keeps the typed text or merges the two.

items.title: Why nobody can demote the note's original owner
items.body:
A co-owner passes `assertCanManageSharing`, because any OWNER row counts as an owner. `upsertCollaborator` then has one extra rule: if the target is the user in `Note.ownerId` and the new permission is not OWNER, it throws **422 INVALID_PERMISSION_CHANGE**. That is the only protection the original owner has (finding F6).

- *Accepted* is true for other collaborators, not for the `ownerId` user.
- *403, only Note.ownerId may manage sharing* is wrong: co-owners may manage sharing.
- *409, more than one OWNER* is wrong: no rule counts OWNER rows.

excerpts.quote: if (collaborator.id === note.ownerId && input.permission !== "OWNER") { throw appError("The note owner must keep OWNER permission.", 422, "INVALID_PERMISSION_CHANGE");

items.title: Why a co-owner can create more co-owners
items.body:
`isOwner` is true for any collaborator whose row is OWNER, not only for the `Note.ownerId` user. So a co-owner passes the sharing check, and `shareNoteSchema` accepts every `NotePermission`, OWNER included. The upsert and its `NOTE_COLLABORATOR_UPSERTED` audit row are written in one transaction. The editor now has an OWNER row and, with it, `canManageSharing` and `canArchive`. The auth doc lists this as finding F6.

- *Only Note.ownerId may grant OWNER* is the fix the doc sketches, not the code.
- *422, OWNER not accepted* is wrong: the enum includes it.
- *Cannot change status* is wrong: `canArchive` is also `isOwner`.

items.title: Why a lost save race leaves no conflict in the audit log
items.body:
There are two conflict paths. The pre-check compares the stored version with `baseVersionNumber`, writes `NOTE_CONFLICT_REJECTED` and throws 409. In the race path the pre-check passed, but the conditional update inside the transaction matched nothing, so the callback returns `null`. The service then throws the same **409 VERSION_CONFLICT**, without any audit call. An admin reading the log under-counts exactly the races (finding F3).

- *409 with an audit row* describes the pre-check path.
- *500* is wrong: matching zero rows is a normal result, not an error.
- *200* is wrong: the null result is turned into a conflict.

items.title: One root key means one invalidation reaches everything
items.body:
Every note query key starts with `"notes"`: the list is `["notes"]`, a detail is `["notes", id]` and its revisions are `["notes", id, "revisions"]`. React Query's filters match by prefix, so invalidating `["notes"]` marks all three stale and refetches each one that is mounted. The share hook's `setQueryData` puts the server's answer into the detail first, but the invalidation flags the detail again, so it is fetched anyway, and the revisions are fetched although sharing does not touch them.

To refresh only the list after writing the detail, the hook could invalidate with `exact: true`, or give the list its own sub-key such as `["notes", "list"]`.

- *Only the revisions* assumes a fresh `setQueryData` protects the detail; it does not.
- *Neither* assumes exact matching, which is not the default.
- *Only the detail* ignores that the revisions key starts with the same prefix.

items.title: Why an archived note can still be shared
items.body:
Archiving changes one capability: `canEdit` becomes false. `canManageSharing` is still `isOwner`, and `assertCanManageSharing` looks only at that flag, not at the note status. So the owner's share goes through, the collaborator row is upserted and the change is audited. The auth doc records this as a partial transition guard (check S6).

- *409 NOTE_ARCHIVED* is the edit path's check; sharing has no status check.
- *403* is wrong: the owner keeps the sharing capability.
- *422 for a non-OWNER grant* is wrong: no rule ties the granted permission to the note status.

items.title: Includes cost one query per relation, not per row
items.body:
With its default relation strategy, Prisma answers a `findMany` with includes in stages: one query for the notes, then one query per included relation that selects by an `IN` list of the parent keys. This list has two includes, the owner and the caller's collaborator row, so 200 notes cost three queries however many rows come back. The collaborators-some filter that scopes the list runs inside the first query as a subquery.

N+1 appears when code loops over the results and queries per row, for example calling `findAccessibleById` for each note in a list. Nothing in this repo does that.

- *401* and *201* count per-row lookups that Prisma does not issue.
- *One* would need the join relation strategy (the relationJoins preview), which this schema does not enable.

readMore.why: The list query and its two includes.

items.title: Seeding the cache from a mutation response
items.body:
The create hook does two things on success. It first awaits an invalidation of `["notes"]`, then writes the created note into `["notes", newId]` with `setQueryData`. When the workspace selects the new note a moment later, its detail query finds fresh data, younger than the 15 s staleTime, and does not fetch. Its revisions query has nothing cached, so it fetches once.

Seeding from a response is the cheap way to make a just-created resource appear instantly; it only covers the keys you seed.

- *Detail and revisions* ignores the seed.
- *Only the detail* has it backwards, and revisions are a separate query.
- *None* assumes the revisions key was seeded too.

items.title: Why a too-short title is a 422
items.body:
`createNoteSchema` requires a trimmed title of at least three characters. `parseSchema` runs `safeParse`, and on failure throws an `AppError` with status **422**, code `VALIDATION_ERROR`, and the flattened zod issues as details. `apiError` passes that status through.

- *400 with the raw error* is wrong twice: the status is 422, and the details are flattened, not the raw zod object.
- *500* is what happens to a malformed JSON body, not to a well-formed body with a bad field.
- *Titles never measured* is wrong: the schema has `min(3)` after `trim()`.

excerpts.quote: throw appError( "The request payload did not match the expected shape.", 422, "VALIDATION_ERROR",

items.title: In zod 4, normalizers run where you write them
items.body:
The share schema writes `z.email().trim().toLowerCase()`. In zod 4, `trim` and `toLowerCase` are steps in the same chain as the format check and run in the written order, so the email check sees the raw input. A leading space makes it fail, and `parseSchema` answers **422 VALIDATION_ERROR** before the service or the user lookup runs. Upper-case letters pass the check and are then lowered, so `Editor@Notes.Local` would work. Writing `z.string().trim().toLowerCase().pipe(z.email())`, or putting `trim()` before the format check, normalizes first.

The browser form never hits this, because an input of type email strips leading and trailing whitespace itself; any other client of the API does.

- *200 after trimming* assumes normalize-then-validate.
- *404 USER_NOT_FOUND* needs the request to reach the lookup.
- *The repository* does no trimming.

readMore.why: How a failed safeParse becomes a 422 with flattened issues.

items.title: Concept: what the browser caches and what a transaction sees
items.body:
The later questions in this pack follow one request further than the route: into the transaction on the server, and back out into the React Query cache in the browser.

On the server, open `src/services/note-service.ts` and find each `$transaction(async (db) => ...)`. For every repository call inside a callback, check whether it receives `db` or falls back to the shared client.

In the browser, start with the key factory at the top of `src/features/notes/hooks/use-notes.ts`, then write down, for each mutation, what its `onSuccess` writes and what it invalidates, in order. Then read `src/features/notes/components/notes-workspace.tsx`: how the draft is tied to a note id and a version number, and what each `catch` branch changes. Finally read the zod schemas in `src/lib/validation/note-schemas.ts` field by field.

excerpts.quote: all: ["notes"] as const, detail: (noteId: string) => ["notes", noteId] as const,

How every hook turns a response into data or an ApiClientError.

items.title: Why an archived note answers 409 even to a viewer
items.body:
`updateNote` loads the note, builds the access level and calls `assertCanEditNote`. That helper tests the note status **first**: if the note is ARCHIVED it throws **409 NOTE_ARCHIVED** "Archived notes must be restored before editing." Only for an ACTIVE note does it go on to check `canEdit` and throw 403. The auth doc points out the odd effect: a viewer, who could never edit, is told to restore the note.

- *403 FORBIDDEN* is what the same viewer gets on an ACTIVE note.
- *404* is wrong: the viewer is a collaborator, so the scoped load finds the note.
- *422* is wrong: the access check happens after a valid body was parsed, and nothing here is about shape.

excerpts.quote: if (access.noteStatus === "ARCHIVED") { throw appError("Archived notes must be restored before editing.", 409, "NOTE_ARCHIVED");

items.title: A shared DTO type checks the producer, not the wire
items.body:
`NoteDetail` lives in `src/types/note.ts` and is used on both sides. The compiler can only enforce it where an object of that type is built, and in this repo that is `toDetailDto`, whose returned literal is annotated as `NoteDetail`. A new required field is therefore a compile error there and nowhere else. The browser side never builds a `NoteDetail`: it names the type in `apiFetch`'s generic, and `apiFetch` returns the parsed body with `as T`, a cast. If the server and client were deployed from different commits, the client would trust a shape nobody checked.

Runtime validation of responses (a zod parse in `apiFetch`) or a shared schema would close that gap.

- *use-notes.ts* only names the type.
- *Nowhere* forgets the annotated literal in the service.
- *The routes* pass the result to `ok()`, which accepts any type.

items.title: Concept: from request to response, and safe saves
items.body:
Every API route follows the same shape, so learn it once.

- `withAuth` in `src/lib/middleware/with-auth.ts` resolves the session from the cookie. Note what it returns when there is none and whether the handler still runs.
- Inside the handler, the body is read with `request.json()` and then checked with `parseSchema`. Read `parseSchema` and `apiError` (`src/lib/http/api-response.ts`) and write down which errors keep their own status and what happens to every other error. Then walk three bodies through the route: a valid one, a well-formed one with a bad field, and one that is not JSON at all.

Next, the save path in `updateNote`. It has a pre-check on `baseVersionNumber` and, inside a transaction, a conditional update. For each of the two ways a stale save can be caught, note the status, the code and every row that gets written. Do the same for `updateStatus` when the requested status equals the current one. The findings list in the auth doc is a good place to compare your notes after you finish.

readMore.why: The authentication wrapper every API route uses.
How a failed zod parse becomes an API error.

items.title: Why logging out with an expired session keeps the cookie
items.body:
The logout route is wrapped in `withAuth`. With an expired or missing session row, `withAuth` resolves `null` and immediately returns **401 UNAUTHENTICATED**; the handler, which would delete the row and call `clearSessionCookie`, never runs. The stale cookie stays in the browser until its own expiry, and nothing in the app removes expired session rows (finding F9).

- *Cleared for stale sessions* is the fix the doc suggests, not today's code.
- *Row deleted* is wrong in both remaining options: the handler that deletes the row is never reached.

items.title: A server-side page guard runs once, at render
items.body:
The `/notes` page checks the session on the server and redirects anonymous visitors, which keeps protected HTML from ever being sent. That check runs when the page renders. Afterwards the page is a client app, and every note it loads comes from API calls. When the session expires, `withAuth` answers those calls with a 401 JSON body, `apiFetch` throws, and the new detail query ends in an error with no data. The workspace shows the editor only when it has data, so the user gets the Choose a note panel, and no code in the client treats 401 as a reason to go to `/login`.

A global `onError` on the query cache that redirects on 401 is the usual fix.

- *The redirect* would need the page to render again.
- *Cached text* needs a note opened earlier in this tab.
- *The banner* shows only save, create and status messages.

readMore.why: What every API route answers when the session is gone.

items.title: Concept: capabilities computed per note
items.body:
Two layers decide what a caller may do.

**System role.** A user is `MEMBER` or `APP_ADMIN`. Only the audit-log route checks the system role, through `withRole` nested inside `withAuth`.

**Note capability.** `getNoteAccessLevel` in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` turns the caller, the note's status and its collaborator rows into `permission`, `canEdit`, `canManageSharing` and `canArchive`. Build the matrix yourself from the code: one row per caller type (admin, the `Note.ownerId` user, another OWNER row, EDITOR, VIEWER, no row), one column per capability, and one table for ACTIVE notes and one for ARCHIVED ones. Note exactly what `isOwner` is made of.

Then read the three assert helpers below it, and for each one note which conditions it tests and **in what order**, and the status and code each throws. Finally, in `note-service.ts`, list for each write method every check that runs before the write, in order, with the status each one throws.

excerpts.quote: `getNoteAccessLevel()` turns the note owner id, note status, and collaborator rows into a single access object

Every note write and its checks.

items.title: Why sharing with an unknown email is 404
items.body:
Once the owner passes the sharing check, `upsertCollaborator` looks the email up with `findByEmail`. No user means **404 USER_NOT_FOUND** "No user with that email exists yet." The app has no sign-up route and no invitation model, so a collaborator must already exist as a user (the seed creates the demo accounts).

- *A pending invitation* is wrong: nothing stores one.
- *422* is wrong: the email passed the schema; the problem is that no account has it.
- *A new user created* is wrong: users exist only through the seed or a manual insert.

excerpts.quote: if (!collaborator) { throw appError("No user with that email exists yet.", 404, "USER_NOT_FOUND");

items.title: Clearing the cache is part of signing out
items.body:
The QueryClient is created once per tab and survives client-side navigation, so without care user A's cached notes would still be there when user B arrives. The logout hook handles it: `onSuccess` awaits `queryClient.clear()`, which drops every cached query, and the workspace navigates to `/login` only after the mutation resolves. B's workspace therefore mounts with an empty cache, and the sidebar is empty until B's own list request returns.

The safeguard depends on the logout request succeeding. If it fails, `onSuccess` never runs and the cache is not cleared.

- *A's notes until staleTime ends* would need the cache to survive.
- *A's notes until a refetch* has the same flaw.
- *Server-embedded notes*: the server page passes only the session.

items.title: Start here: Collab Notes and its docs
items.body:
Collab Notes is a collaborative notes app in Next.js, Prisma and PostgreSQL. Users sign in with a cookie-backed session, share notes per person as OWNER, EDITOR or VIEWER, save with a version number so concurrent edits are detected, archive and restore notes, and admins can read an audit log.

Read in this order:

1. `README.md` for what the app is and what local setup really needs.
2. `docs/learning/guided-reading-path.md` for a route through the code.
3. `docs/architecture/auth-and-permissions.md`: the session flow, the route gate table, the capability matrix and the numbered findings.
4. `docs/architecture/request-lifecycle.md` and `domain-model.md` for every request path and the schema.

The architecture docs mark each finding as run or read-only. Keep `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` and `src/services/note-service.ts` open as you read: almost every quiz question is decided by one of the checks in those two files.

excerpts.quote: a collaborative notes app with cookie-backed sessions, per-note sharing
